name: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)
intent: Keep business rules free of databases, vendors and web frameworks by making the core define the interfaces it needs, and letting adapters at the edge implement them, so that infrastructure can be swapped and rules can be tested without it.
scenario: An order service has three use cases: place an order, cancel an order and report on orders. Each one calls the SQL client, the payment vendor's SDK and the mail client directly, so switching the payment vendor edits 3 files, with 6 unrelated behaviours sitting beside the change. The team introduces ports and adapters, and the same switch edits 2 files. Then the port is written to mirror the vendor's own API, and the switch edits 5 files again. Another team puts every small thing behind a port and a mapper, and adding one field to an order edits 7 files.
problem: In a layered design the business rules usually depend on the code below them: the use case imports the database client and the vendor SDK, so their details leak upward and the rules cannot run without them. Hexagonal architecture turns that around. The core states what it needs as ports (interfaces in the language of the domain), and adapters at the edge implement them for a specific database, vendor or protocol, so the dependency arrows point inward. This only works if the port says what the domain needs, not what one vendor offers. A port shaped like the vendor's API leaks as much as a direct call, and a port for every small thing adds files without absorbing any change. Practitioners disagree on how much to abstract: some put a port at every boundary, others only where a second implementation or a test double is likely.

howItWorks.title: Put the rules in the core
howItWorks.text: The core holds the domain model and the use cases: what an order is, when shipping is free, what cancelling does. It has no import of a database client, an HTTP framework or a vendor SDK, so it can be read, tested and changed without any of them.

howItWorks.title: Define ports in the core's language
howItWorks.text: A port is an interface the core owns. It says what the core needs (save this order, charge this amount) in domain terms. Driving ports are what the outside calls (place an order); driven ports are what the core calls (a payment gateway, an order store). The core owns both kinds, and that ownership is what points the dependency arrows inward.

howItWorks.title: Write adapters at the edge
howItWorks.text: An adapter translates between a port and one technology: an HTTP adapter turns a request into a use case call, a SQL adapter turns a save into queries, a vendor adapter turns a charge into the vendor's SDK calls. Adapters depend on the core, never the other way round, and each one holds the details of exactly one technology.

howItWorks.title: Wire everything at one place
howItWorks.text: A composition root, often the program's main function, creates the adapters and hands them to the use cases. Swapping the database or the vendor then means writing a new adapter and changing that one wiring place, and the rules are not touched. In tests the same place plugs in in-memory fakes.

howItWorks.title: Keep the port honest and the count small
howItWorks.text: Check each port against a real change or a real test: if no second implementation or test double is plausible, the abstraction may only add files. And check that the port does not mirror the vendor: if the core reads a vendor's status codes, a vendor swap edits the core anyway.

pros: Business rules can be tested with in-memory fakes, with no database or network
Swapping a database, vendor or framework edits one adapter and the wiring, not the rules
The dependency direction is explicit, so infrastructure details cannot creep into the rules unnoticed
Several entry points (HTTP, a queue consumer, a command line) can share the same use cases
cons: More files and more translation code: ports, adapters, mappers and a composition root
The ports are a design judgement, and a wrong one (too thin, too vendor-shaped) costs as much as no port
Simple create-read-update-delete features gain little, and still pay for the structure
Rules that depend on database features (transactions, locking, query planning) leak through any port
whenToUse: The rules are the valuable and long-lived part, and the database, vendor or framework is likely to change around them
You want fast tests of the rules without infrastructure, using fakes
The same rules are reached by several entry points or backed by several kinds of storage
whenNotToUse: A thin CRUD service or script where the rules are few and the database is the point
A short-lived prototype whose infrastructure will not change
As a rule that every boundary needs a port, including ones where no second implementation or fake will ever exist
pitfalls: A port shaped like the vendor's API (its method names, flags and status codes), so a vendor swap edits the core and the port as well as the adapter
A port for everything, plus a mapper between every pair of layers, so adding one field to an order edits 7 files
Ports with exactly one implementation and no test double, which add a file and a hop and absorb no change
Leaking infrastructure through the types: the core passing database rows, ORM entities or HTTP request objects across the port
Hiding a capability the rules really need, such as a transaction, behind a port that cannot express it, then working around the port
Believing the structure makes a swap free: the new adapter still has to match the old one's behaviour, and that needs tests against the real system
Treating the hexagon as a layer diagram with the database at the bottom, instead of the core owning the interfaces

roles.label: Product
roles.description: Asks for changes to the order service.

roles.label: Core
roles.description: The domain model and use cases, with no infrastructure imports.

roles.label: Ports
roles.description: Interfaces the core owns and describes in domain terms.

roles.label: Adapters
roles.description: Code at the edge that speaks to one database, vendor or protocol.

roles.label: Developer
roles.description: Makes the change and re-tests what it touched.

quiz.question: In a hexagonal design, which way do the source-code dependencies point between the core and a SQL adapter?
options: The core imports the SQL adapter, because it needs to save orders.
Both import each other so that they stay in sync.
Neither depends on the other; they talk through a shared database schema.
The SQL adapter imports the core's port and implements it; the core does not know the adapter exists.
quiz.explanation: The core owns the port and the adapter implements it, so the dependency points inward. That is why the core can be tested and changed without the adapter, and the database can be replaced by writing a new adapter.

quiz.question: A team defines a payment port with the vendor's own method names and status codes, and the use case checks those codes. The vendor is replaced. What happens?
options: Only the adapter changes, because a port always isolates the vendor.
The use case, the port and the adapter all change, so the port gave no protection.
Nothing changes, because the vendor behind the port is invisible.
Only the wiring changes, because adapters are interchangeable.
quiz.explanation: A port protects the core only if it is written in the core's own terms. When it copies the vendor's vocabulary, the vendor's details are part of the core and a swap edits it, which costs as much as calling the vendor directly.

quiz.question: Which signal most suggests that a design has too many ports and adapters?
options: The rules can be tested without a database.
The composition root is the only place that creates adapters.
Adding a single field to an order edits a request mapper, a persistence mapper and a persistence model, besides the real work.
A second entry point reuses the same use cases.
quiz.explanation: Mappers that only copy a record between layers absorb no change. Each one has to be edited for every field, so the cost of an ordinary change grows with the number of layers while the swaps it was built for stay rare.
